identification.summary: SharpPanda (Check Point Research later renamed it Sharp Dragon) is a China-linked espionage actor that Check Point named in 2021 after analyzing a previously unknown backdoor used against a Southeast Asian government [S1][S4]. Cyble describes it as active since at least 2018 [S3]. Check Point assessed the 2021 operation was carried out by a Chinese APT group that had been testing and refining its tools for at least three years [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Cyble: active since at least 2018 [S3]. Check Point named the group in June 2021 and says its Soul framework has been in use since at least 2017 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Check Point now uses the name Sharp Dragon for the actor formerly called Sharp Panda [S4]. No Microsoft Typhoon/Storm name was found in the sources gathered. Some secondary summaries equate Sharp Panda with APT19, Emissary Panda or Iron Tiger; this was not confirmed by any primary vendor source I could open and should not be assumed.

attribution.confidence: Vendor assessment only: Check Point describes the actor as Chinese [S1][S4]. Check Point added that it cannot exclude that the Soul framework is used by multiple threat actors in the region [S2]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Check Point analysis of malware (VictoryDll, SoulSearcher, Soul), lures and targeting [S1][S2][S4]. Reporting that the 2021 backdoor ran only during Chinese working hours appears in secondary summaries and was not verified in a primary source.

objectives: Espionage against government organizations, inferred from the targeting of a Southeast Asian foreign ministry-level government entity, G20 government officials and African and Caribbean governments [S1][S3][S4]. No source states the sponsor's specific requirements.

regions: Southeast Asia (Check Point: historically Vietnam, Thailand and Indonesia) [S2]
targeting.notes: Check Point reports a shift in 2024 from Southeast Asia to governmental organizations in Africa and the Caribbean, with the actor using trusted government entities to reach new ones [S4]. A secondary source dates this shift to November 2023 [S6].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with Word/RTF lures that pull remote templates weaponized with the RoyalRoad builder, which exploits Equation Editor vulnerabilities [S1][S2][S3]. 2021: VictoryDll backdoor with file manipulation, process and service enumeration, screenshots and cmd.exe command execution [S1]. 2022-23: SoulSearcher loader fetched from a server that answers only requests from the target country's IP addresses, then the modular Soul framework with a configurable 'radio silence' option [S2][S5]. 2023 G20 campaign: RTF exploitation, DLL loader, scheduled-task persistence and system information collection [S3]. 2024: compromised a high-profile email account to send lures, exploited 1-day vulnerabilities to compromise servers later used as C2, and deployed Cobalt Strike Beacon instead of custom backdoors [S4]. The Hacker News reports later chains using executables disguised as documents [S6].

campaigns.name: Southeast Asian government, VictoryDll backdoor
campaigns.summary: Check Point reports spear-phishing of employees of a Southeast Asian government entity, using RoyalRoad RTF templates to deliver the previously unknown VictoryDll backdoor.

campaigns.name: Soul framework campaign
campaigns.summary: Check Point observed a campaign in late 2022 against a high-profile Southeast Asian government entity using a new version of the SoulSearcher loader and the Soul modular framework (reported March 2023).

campaigns.name: G20 government officials campaign
campaigns.summary: Cyble reports spam emails carrying a Word document themed on a G7 food security statement, leading to a RoyalRoad RTF, a DLL loader and scheduled-task persistence.

campaigns.name: Expansion to Africa and the Caribbean begins
campaigns.summary: A secondary source dates the start of targeting of African and Caribbean governments to November 2023, facilitated by previously compromised entities in Southeast Asia.

campaigns.name: Sharp Dragon Africa and Caribbean campaign
campaigns.summary: Check Point reports a compromised high-profile email account used to send RoyalRoad lures that deploy Cobalt Strike Beacon against governments in Africa and the Caribbean.

diamond.adversary: China-linked espionage actor named SharpPanda by Check Point in 2021 and renamed Sharp Dragon [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: RoyalRoad weaponized documents, VictoryDll, SoulSearcher and Soul, then Cobalt Strike Beacon [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Geofenced download servers that respond only to the target country's IP addresses [S2]; 1-day-exploited compromised servers reused as C2 [S4]; compromised government email accounts as phishing senders [S4].
diamond.victim: Government organizations in Southeast Asia, G20 nations, Africa and the Caribbean [S1][S2][S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Not stated in sources; targeting of foreign ministries and government officials is consistent with political intelligence collection (analyst inference).
diamond.technology: Microsoft Office Equation Editor vulnerabilities in unpatched Office installations, and email trust relationships between government entities [S1][S4].

gaps: No government attribution or named sponsoring organization found.
Microsoft naming and MITRE ATT&CK group mapping not found; the record has no MITRE group id.
Claimed overlaps with APT19, Emissary Panda, Iron Tiger, Naikon or Cyclops appear only in unverified secondary summaries or were not found; do not merge clusters.
Check Point (2021, 2023, 2024), Cyble, BSI and Rewterz primary pages could not be fetched (host blocked); details rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
Whether the June 2023 Cyble G20 campaign delivered Soul is not confirmed.
The 'Chinese working hours' backdoor behavior is from secondary summaries only.
Victim counts, named victims and exfiltrated data are not public in the sources gathered.
Activity after May 2024 was not found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Government email systems and foreign-ministry networks are key terrain, as are compromised servers and accounts that let the actor send lures from trusted senders [S1][S4]. STEP 2: The actor reuses old Equation Editor exploits, so unpatched Office installs and legacy documents are the exploitable weakness [S1][S3]. STEP 3: Observed template is a phishing email, RoyalRoad document, loader, then backdoor or Cobalt Strike, with C2 geofencing that limits sandbox and researcher visibility [S2][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued spear-phishing of government and diplomatic targets, including coalition or partner governments in Africa, Southeast Asia and the Caribbean [S4]. MDCOA is use of a compromised partner-government mailbox to phish US or allied personnel during a crisis, evading sender-reputation filters [S4]. Candidate indicators: Word documents fetching remote RTF templates, Equation Editor child processes, new scheduled tasks created by Office-launched DLLs, Cobalt Strike Beacon traffic to recently compromised servers, and C2 that answers only from in-country IPs [S2][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track partner-nation government compromises as a precursor to lures reaching US and coalition mailboxes [S4]. (2) Authorities: coordinate sharing of indicators with partner governments through approved channels before action on partner-owned infrastructure. (3) Mission assurance: disable Equation Editor and block remote-template loading in Office on mission networks; prioritize email gateways handling coalition correspondence [S1][S3]. (4) Coordination: because C2 is geofenced, hunt teams should request sandbox detonation from in-region sensors and share findings with the relevant cyber defense providers.

provenance.importedSummary: SharpPanda, an APT group originating from China, has seen a rise in its cyber-attack operations starting from at least 2018. The APT group utilizes spear-phishing techniques to obtain initial access, employing a combination of outdated Microsoft Office document vulnerabilities, novel evasion techniques, and highly potent backdoor malware.
